lead: Detailing turns the steel calculated for bending, shear and torsion into a drawing a site team can build. Every bar gets a diameter, position, length, shape and anchorage. The drawing must keep cover, bar spacing, stirrup spacing, hooks, bends, development length and lap lengths within code limits. A correct design with poor detailing can crack, spall or fail at a lap. Some syllabi call this 'detailing requirements'. It is used on every beam, slab and column drawing and in the bar bending schedule that the contractor uses to cut and bend steel.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 for stirrups, 3.3 for torsion steel, 3.5 for Ld and 3.6 for laps and curtailment.

blocks.text: Cover is concrete between the surface and the steel. It protects steel from water and fire and gives bond. Nominal cover is the cover written on the drawing, measured to the outer surface of the outermost steel, usually the stirrup. Clear cover is the least actual concrete thickness to a bar surface. For a main bar inside a stirrup, clear cover = nominal cover + stirrup diameter. Do not use nominal cover as clear cover in spacing checks.

For n bars in one layer in a beam of width b, the clear spacing s is s = (b − 2c − 2φ<sub>s</sub> − nφ)/(n − 1). Here b is the beam width in mm, c is nominal cover to the outside of the stirrup in mm, φ<sub>s</sub> is stirrup bar diameter in mm, φ is main bar diameter in mm and n is the number of bars. The minimum clear spacing is the greatest of φ, 25 mm and (maximum aggregate size + 5 mm).

When bars are in two layers, the vertical clear gap between layers must be at least the greater of 15 mm and the nominal maximum size of coarse aggregate. Keep the largest bars at the corners. If spacing fails, increase width, use a larger bar with fewer bars, or put bars in two layers with a clear gap meeting that limit. The worked example below checks a 300 mm beam with four 16 mm bars.

A stirrup is a closed tie. Its spacing is closest near the support, where shear is high, and may increase toward mid-span as shear falls. Show the first stirrup at 50 mm from the support face unless the drawing gives another value. At a curtailment point, keep stirrups close on both sides because a stopped bar needs anchorage and the section is disturbed.

Hooks transfer force into concrete. A 90° bend alone can open under load; use a 135° hook for stirrups in beams, with the hook enclosing a longitudinal bar. Bend bars around a mandrel. Sharp bends crush concrete inside the bend and crack the bar. Code rules give a minimum internal bend radius as a multiple of bar diameter, larger for larger bars. Do not rebend a bar at the same place on site.

The drawing shows stirrup diameter, shape, hook length and spacing mark. A common mark is '8 φ @ 150 c/c near support, 8 φ @ 200 c/c at mid-span'. Define φ as bar diameter and c/c as centre-to-centre. The schedule gives each stirrup's cutting length: centreline perimeter plus hook allowance. Check that the stirrup fits inside cover and around the main bars.

sections.h3: Anchorage, laps and the bar schedule

blocks.text: A bar force cannot stop at a section. It must be carried into concrete by development length Ld, or into another bar by a lap. Ld comes from Chapter 3.5. A tension lap is at least the greater of Ld and 30φ unless a code rule says otherwise; a compression lap is shorter. Show every lap length as a dimension on the drawing, not as a note 'lap'. Stagger laps: do not put all laps at one section.

Curtailment stops a bar where bending moment has fallen. The bar must extend beyond the theoretical cut-off by L<sub>d</sub>, and enough bars must continue to the support. Keep some bottom steel continuous into the support as the code requires in a beam. For a cantilever, top steel must develop into the support. The drawing marks the cut-off point and the extension.

items: Draw in this order: (1) mark beam size, cover and stirrup; (2) place main bars to scale and check clear spacing; (3) mark stirrup spacing zones; (4) dimension L<sub>d</sub>, laps and curtailment; (5) write bar marks; (6) fill the bar bending schedule.

blocks.text: A bar bending schedule lists bar mark, diameter, shape, number, cutting length and weight. Weight per metre = φ²/162 kg/m for φ in mm. For a 16 mm bar this is about 1.58 kg/m. The BBS and drawing must agree: every bar on the drawing appears in the schedule with a length and a position. The contractor cuts and bends from the BBS, so one missing lap length becomes a site error.

figure.caption: From outside inward: 25 mm nominal cover, 8 mm stirrup, 16 mm main bar, and a 56.7 mm clear gap between main bars. The gap is larger than the 25 mm minimum.

spec.aria: From outside inward, a beam section has 25 mm nominal cover, an 8 mm stirrup, a 16 mm main bar, and 56.7 mm clear spacing between bars.

examples.question: A beam is 300 mm wide with four 16 mm bars in one layer, 8 mm stirrups and 25 mm nominal cover to the outside of the stirrup. Check the clear spacing between bars and state if the layout is valid.
steps: Total width of four main bars = nφ = 4×16 = 64 mm.
For normal 20 mm aggregate, minimum clear spacing = max(φ, 25 mm, aggregate + 5 mm) = max(16, 25, 25) = 25 mm.
56.7 mm is greater than 25 mm, so the bars fit with a clear gap.
examples.answer: The clear spacing is 56.7 mm, which is greater than the 25 mm minimum, so the layout is valid.
examples.check:
b = 300
c = 25
phi_s = 8
n = 4
phi = 16
inside = b - 2*c - 2*phi_s
steel = n*phi
s = (inside - steel)/(n - 1)
smin = max(phi, 25, 20 + 5)
print(inside)
print(steel)
print(round(s, 1))
print(smin)

traps: Using nominal cover as clear cover. If the drawing says 25 mm nominal and the stirrup is 8 mm, the clear cover to the main bar is 33 mm, not 25 mm.
Forgetting the stirrup diameter in spacing: subtract 2c and 2φ<sub>s</sub> before dividing by (n − 1).
Showing a lap as a note without its length. A lap has a dimension and a stagger.
Curtailing a bar exactly at the theoretical cut-off. Extend it by L<sub>d</sub> beyond that point.
Mixing weight formula units: φ²/162 gives kg/m only when φ is in mm.

quiz.q: Define nominal cover and clear cover.
quiz.a: Nominal cover is the specified cover to the outer surface of the outermost steel, usually the stirrup. Clear cover is the least concrete thickness to a bar surface.

quiz.q: Why is the first stirrup placed close to the support?
quiz.a: Shear is highest at the support. Close stirrups resist diagonal cracking there and anchor the first section of the beam.

quiz.q: A 250 mm wide beam has three 20 mm bars, 8 mm stirrups and 25 mm clear cover to the stirrup. Find the clear spacing.
quiz.a: Inside width = 250 − 2×25 − 2×8 = 184 mm. Steel width = 3×20 = 60 mm. Clear spacing = (184 − 60)/(3 − 1) = 62 mm. Minimum is max(20, 25) = 25 mm, so it is valid.

quiz.q: Why must a curtailed bar extend L<sub>d</sub> beyond the theoretical cut-off?
quiz.a: At the cut-off the bar may still carry force. The extension develops that force into concrete before the bar ends, preventing a sudden pull-out.

quiz.q: Find the weight per metre of a 16 mm bar.
What must a bar bending schedule contain?
quiz.a: Bar mark, diameter, shape, number of bars, cutting length and weight, matching the drawing.

quiz.q: Site pushes the main bars outward so the cover is reduced and the clear gap between bars shrinks. Which checks fail, and what should be done?
quiz.a: Nominal cover falls below the specified value, so durability and fire protection fail. Clear spacing falls below the minimum (greatest of bar diameter, 25 mm, aggregate + 5 mm), so concrete cannot be placed properly. Effective depth also changes. Reject the layout and reset the bars to the drawing.

beyond: Not for the exam. Detailing is now checked in BIM models and by bar-bending software that exports cutting lists to bending machines. Fabricators use couplers and headed bars where laps would be too long. Site teams scan bar marks with phones to match bundles to drawings. Search 'IS 456 detailing clauses', 'bar bending schedule cutting length' and 'mechanical splice' to go further.
